    Reading GEOS cubed-sphere grids with pyramids-mesh¶

    GEOS (the NASA Goddard Earth Observing System model) runs on a cubed-sphere grid: the sphere is tiled by six square panels, each a C x C array of cells. The native NetCDF-4 file stores the panel corners as corner_lons/corner_lats of shape (6, C+1, C+1); the driver reconstructs the quadrilateral connectivity by index arithmetic across the six panels.

    This notebook reads the C12 test grid (6 × 12 × 12 = 864 cells) into a pyramids MeshDataset. A nice property falls out later: because the panels are stitched only within each face, connected_components recovers the six cube panels. Coordinates are in degrees.

    2. Imports¶

    The import below is all the setup this adds: MeshDataset is the object every driver hands back (a Mesh2d or Mesh1d wrapper). Importing from pyramids also puts its vendored GDAL/PROJ data in place for you, so nothing about it is order-sensitive in a notebook -- just import the names you use.

    In [1]:
    Copied! 
    from pyramids.netcdf.ugrid import MeshDataset
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from cleopatra.basemap.tiles import add_tiles
    from pyramids.netcdf.ugrid import MeshDataset import numpy as np import pandas as pd from cleopatra.basemap.tiles import add_tiles

    3. Locate the example file¶

    This notebook lives in docs/examples/, so examples/data/ is two levels up. The GEOS sample is geos/test-c12.native.nc4, a C12 cubed-sphere grid (NetCDF-4) from the UXarray test suite.

    Paths inside a notebook are always written relative to the notebook itself, and pyramids' read_file accepts a pathlib.Path directly — we pass the Path, never str(path).

    In [2]:
    Copied! 
    from pathlib import Path
DATA = Path("../../examples/data")
mesh_file = DATA / "geos" / "test-c12.native.nc4"
mesh_file, mesh_file.exists()
    from pathlib import Path DATA = Path("../../examples/data") mesh_file = DATA / "geos" / "test-c12.native.nc4" mesh_file, mesh_file.exists()
    Out[2]:
    (WindowsPath('../../examples/data/geos/test-c12.native.nc4'), True)

    4. Read the mesh¶

    MeshDataset.read_file(path, driver="geos") dispatches the file to the geos driver, which parses it and hands back a MeshDataset — the same pyramids type produced from a native UGRID NetCDF file. We name the driver explicitly here because several formats share the .nc4 suffix; read_file can auto-detect, but being explicit is unambiguous.

    In [3]:
    Copied! 
    ds = MeshDataset.read_file(mesh_file, driver="geos")
type(ds).__name__
    ds = MeshDataset.read_file(mesh_file, driver="geos") type(ds).__name__

  driver = _instantiate(entry_point)
C:\python-environments\worktrees\pyramids-mesh\example-notebooks\src\pyramids_mesh\_base.py:484: UserWarning: 26 clockwise face(s) were reversed to counter-clockwise; a writer will emit the corrected order
  parsed = validate_and_normalise(parsed)
    Out[3]:

    Copied! 
    from cleopatra.config import Config
Config.set_matplotlib_backend()

    5. Explore the dataset¶

    A MeshDataset exposes summary properties describing the whole mesh: n_node / n_face (size), crs / epsg (georeferencing, if the format recorded any), bounds (spatial extent), and data_variable_names (any attached fields).

    In [5]:
    Copied! 
    pd.Series({
    "n_node": ds.n_node,
    "n_face": ds.n_face,
    "crs": ds.crs,
    "epsg": ds.epsg,
    "bounds": ds.bounds,
    "data_variable_names": ds.data_variable_names,
})
    pd.Series({ "n_node": ds.n_node, "n_face": ds.n_face, "crs": ds.crs, "epsg": ds.epsg, "bounds": ds.bounds, "data_variable_names": ds.data_variable_names, })
    Out[5]:
    n_node                                                              1014
n_face                                                               864
crs                                                                 None
epsg                                                                None
bounds                 (0.35864555835723877, -90.0, 358.2829895019531...
data_variable_names                                                   []
dtype: object

    864 quadrilateral faces (6 panels × 12 × 12) on 1014 nodes. crs/epsg are None and data_variable_names is empty — a native grid description with no fields. The bounds reaching −90 → 90 latitude flag degree coordinates.

    6. Coordinates are in DEGREES¶

    GEOS corner coordinates are stored in degrees of longitude/latitude. The ranges confirm it: longitude roughly 0 → 358, latitude the full −90 → 90.

    In [6]:
    Copied! 
    nx, ny = ds.mesh.node_x, ds.mesh.node_y
pd.Series({
    "node_x min/max": (float(nx.min()), float(nx.max())),
    "node_y min/max": (float(ny.min()), float(ny.max())),
    "two_pi": float(2*np.pi), "half_pi": float(np.pi/2),
})
    nx, ny = ds.mesh.node_x, ds.mesh.node_y pd.Series({ "node_x min/max": (float(nx.min()), float(nx.max())), "node_y min/max": (float(ny.min()), float(ny.max())), "two_pi": float(2*np.pi), "half_pi": float(np.pi/2), })
    Out[6]:
    node_x min/max    (0.35864555835723877, 358.2829895019531)
node_y min/max                               (-90.0, 90.0)
two_pi                                            6.283185
half_pi                                           1.570796
dtype: object

    node_y spans the full −90 → 90 and node_x nearly the full circle in degrees — no radian conversion needed; assign a geographic CRS before CRS-aware operations.

    7. The underlying Mesh2d topology¶

    ds.mesh is the Mesh2d holding the raw topology. The arrays you reach for most often are node_x/node_y (node coordinates), face_node_connectivity.data — the (n_face, k) table listing the node indices of each face — and face_areas (one value per face).

    In [7]:
    Copied! 
    mesh = ds.mesh
cx, cy = mesh.face_centroids
conn = mesh.face_node_connectivity.data
{
    "n_node": int(mesh.node_x.shape[0]),
    "connectivity_shape": conn.shape,
    "face_areas_shape": mesh.face_areas.shape,
    "face_centroids_shape": (cx.shape, cy.shape),
}
    mesh = ds.mesh cx, cy = mesh.face_centroids conn = mesh.face_node_connectivity.data { "n_node": int(mesh.node_x.shape[0]), "connectivity_shape": conn.shape, "face_areas_shape": mesh.face_areas.shape, "face_centroids_shape": (cx.shape, cy.shape), }
    Out[7]:
    {'n_node': 1014,
 'connectivity_shape': (864, 4),
 'face_areas_shape': (864,),
 'face_centroids_shape': ((864,), (864,))}

    The connectivity shape is (864, 4): four nodes per cell — cubed-sphere cells are quadrilaterals. 864 = 6 × 12 × 12, the six panels of a C12 grid. The k = 4 is why circumcenters will not apply.

    8. The wireframe¶

    The simplest visualization needs no data — just draw the cell edges. plot_outline() renders the mesh skeleton through cleopatra; it is the fastest sanity check that a file read in correctly.

    In [8]:
    Copied! 
    _g = ds.plot_outline()
if ds.epsg:
    add_tiles(_g.ax, crs=ds.epsg)
    _g = ds.plot_outline() if ds.epsg: add_tiles(_g.ax, crs=ds.epsg)

    The wireframe shows the six cube panels unrolled onto the lon/lat plane. The seams between panels are visible — and are exactly why the connected-components count comes out as six below.

    9. A data map: per-cell area¶

    A native GEOS grid file carries no field values, so we synthesise one. We compute each cell's area from the geometry and attach it as a face-located variable with with_variable(...), which returns a new dataset (the original ds is left untouched). Colouring by it produces the generic pyramids data-map that any per-cell field (depth, velocity, …) would use.

    In [9]:
    Copied! 
    d2 = ds.with_variable("face_area", mesh.face_areas, location="face")
_g = d2.plot("face_area", cmap="viridis", colorbar=True, title="Per-cell area")
if ds.epsg:
    add_tiles(_g.ax, crs=ds.epsg)
    d2 = ds.with_variable("face_area", mesh.face_areas, location="face") _g = d2.plot("face_area", cmap="viridis", colorbar=True, title="Per-cell area") if ds.epsg: add_tiles(_g.ax, crs=ds.epsg)

    Each quad is shaded by area (degree-squared units), brighter near the equator and dimmer toward the poles — the standard lon/lat area distortion, here across all six panels.

    summary() reports per-variable statistics (count, min, max, mean, std) for every attached field.

    In [10]:
    Copied! 
    d2.summary()
    d2.summary()
    Out[10]:
    count min max mean std
    variable
    face_area 864 38.748477 2841.157155 135.443383 388.02755

    The single face_area row (count = 864) captures the size spread across panels and latitudes.

    10. GIS operations, for free¶

    Because the mesh is a pyramids object, the pyramids GIS layer applies directly — none of these methods live in pyramids-mesh. We tour a few.

    Faces as a GeoDataFrame¶

    to_geodataframe() turns every face into a polygon row of a geopandas GeoDataFrame — the standard vector structure for export to shapefile/GeoPackage or for spatial joins.

    In [11]:
    Copied! 
    gdf = ds.to_geodataframe()
gdf.head()
    gdf = ds.to_geodataframe() gdf.head()
    Out[11]:
    geometry
    0 POLYGON ((305 -35.264, 311.465 -38.033, 311.46...
    1 POLYGON ((311.465 -38.033, 318.4 -40.422, 318....
    2 POLYGON ((318.4 -40.422, 325.797 -42.368, 325....
    3 POLYGON ((325.797 -42.368, 333.602 -43.811, 33...
    4 POLYGON ((333.602 -43.811, 341.717 -44.7, 341....

    One row per face, each carrying its cell polygon. Plotting the GeoDataFrame directly with geopandas draws every face as a filled polygon — a second, vector-native view of the same mesh.

    In [12]:
    Copied! 
    ax = gdf.plot(edgecolor="black", linewidth=0.2, facecolor="#cfe8ef")
if ds.epsg:
    add_tiles(ax, crs=ds.epsg)
    ax = gdf.plot(edgecolor="black", linewidth=0.2, facecolor="#cfe8ef") if ds.epsg: add_tiles(ax, crs=ds.epsg)

    One quadrilateral cell per row, across all six panels. CRS unset; assign a geographic CRS before export.

    Bounding polygon¶

    bounding_polygon() dissolves the cells into the outer boundary. For the unrolled global C12 grid it returns a shapely Polygon.

    In [13]:
    Copied! 
    poly = ds.bounding_polygon()
{"type": type(poly).__name__, "bounds": ds.bounds}
    poly = ds.bounding_polygon() {"type": type(poly).__name__, "bounds": ds.bounds}
    Out[13]:
    {'type': 'Polygon',
 'bounds': (0.35864555835723877, -90.0, 358.2829895019531, 90.0)}

    A single Polygon of the global extent — a plain shapely geometry for clipping or export.

    Circumcenters — not applicable¶

    circumcenters() is defined only for triangular meshes. GEOS is a quadrilateral mesh, so calling it raises ValueError: circumcenters is only defined for triangular meshes. We show the guard rather than force it — a circumcenter has no unique definition for a polygon with more than three sides.

    In [14]:
    Copied! 
    try:
    ds.circumcenters()
except ValueError as e:
    print("skipped:", e)
    try: ds.circumcenters() except ValueError as e: print("skipped:", e)
    skipped: circumcenters is only defined for triangular meshes.

    Expected: the operation is simply undefined for this cell shape. A triangular dual mesh would be the prerequisite for finite-volume circumcenter schemes on this grid.

    Boundary edges and face adjacency¶

    exterior_edges() returns the indices of the edges that lie on the mesh boundary (each interior edge is shared by two faces; a boundary edge by one). sparse_adjacency() returns the face–face adjacency as a SciPy sparse matrix — the graph a flow solver walks.

    In [15]:
    Copied! 
    ee = ds.exterior_edges()
adj = ds.sparse_adjacency()
{
    "n_boundary_edges": int(ee.shape[0]),
    "adjacency_shape": adj.shape,
    "adjacency_nnz": int(adj.nnz),
}
    ee = ds.exterior_edges() adj = ds.sparse_adjacency() { "n_boundary_edges": int(ee.shape[0]), "adjacency_shape": adj.shape, "adjacency_nnz": int(adj.nnz), }
    Out[15]:
    {'n_boundary_edges': 288, 'adjacency_shape': (864, 864), 'adjacency_nnz': 3168}

    The (864, 864) adjacency matrix records in-panel neighbours; the large boundary-edge count is the key clue to the next result — because cells are stitched only within each panel, every panel edge counts as a boundary, leaving the six panels mutually disconnected.

    Connected components¶

    connected_components() labels each face by which connected piece of the adjacency graph it belongs to. The number of distinct labels tells you whether the mesh is one contiguous surface or several disjoint pieces.

    In [16]:
    Copied! 
    labels = ds.connected_components()
n_comp = int(np.unique(labels).size)
{"n_components": n_comp, "counts": np.bincount(labels).tolist()}
    labels = ds.connected_components() n_comp = int(np.unique(labels).size) {"n_components": n_comp, "counts": np.bincount(labels).tolist()}
    Out[16]:
    {'n_components': 6, 'counts': [144, 144, 144, 144, 144, 144]}

    Six components — one per cube panel. The driver stitches connectivity within each panel but not across the cube seams, so connected_components recovers the cubed-sphere's six faces exactly. The counts are 144 each (12 × 12): a striking, geometry-revealing result.

    Cropping to a bounding box¶

    crop(bbox=(xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax)) returns a new MeshDataset holding only the faces inside the box — the mesh equivalent of a spatial window. (subset_by_bounds(xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax) does the same with positional arguments.) We crop to one quadrant of the extent and plot the result.

    In [17]:
    Copied! 
    b = ds.bounds
bbox = (b[0], b[1], (b[0]+b[2])/2, (b[1]+b[3])/2)
cropped = ds.crop(bbox=bbox)
_g = cropped.plot_outline()
if ds.epsg:
    add_tiles(_g.ax, crs=ds.epsg)
    b = ds.bounds bbox = (b[0], b[1], (b[0]+b[2])/2, (b[1]+b[3])/2) cropped = ds.crop(bbox=bbox) _g = cropped.plot_outline() if ds.epsg: add_tiles(_g.ax, crs=ds.epsg)

    Cropping to one quadrant of the degree extent keeps the cells in that lon/lat window — typically spanning parts of several panels that happen to fall in the box.

    Writing the mesh back out¶

    to_file(path, driver=...) serialises the mesh through any write-capable driver. We round-trip to Stanford PLY (driver="ply"), which stores arbitrary polygon faces, into a temp file and read it back to confirm the topology survived.

    In [18]:
    Copied! 
    import tempfile
out = Path(tempfile.gettempdir()) / "geos_roundtrip.ply"
ds.to_file(out, driver="ply")
back = MeshDataset.read_file(out, driver="ply")
{"wrote_bytes": out.stat().st_size, "n_face_back": back.n_face, "matches": back.n_face == ds.n_face}
    import tempfile out = Path(tempfile.gettempdir()) / "geos_roundtrip.ply" ds.to_file(out, driver="ply") back = MeshDataset.read_file(out, driver="ply") {"wrote_bytes": out.stat().st_size, "n_face_back": back.n_face, "matches": back.n_face == ds.n_face}
    Out[18]:
    {'wrote_bytes': 54876, 'n_face_back': 864, 'matches': True}

    The face count survives the round-trip: the mesh we read from a GEOS grid wrote cleanly to a different format and came back identical. PLY is used because this format's own driver is read-only — to_file dispatches to whichever driver advertises a write capability.

    11. What we cannot do here, and why¶

    Two pyramids operations are unavailable on this mesh, and the reasons are instructive:

    • to_crs(epsg) — skipped. This grid carries no CRS (crs is None above), so pyramids refuses to reproject: to_crs raises "Cannot reproject: source CRS is unknown." You would first assign the known CRS (these global grids are geographic lon/lat on a sphere) and only then reproject.
    • rasterize_like(...) / regrid(...) — out of scope here. Burning the mesh onto a raster grid or remapping between meshes is a genuine pyramids capability, but it needs a target raster/mesh and a resampling choice to be meaningful — a topic for a dedicated regridding tutorial, not this format tour.

    Note — xarray interop. pyramids-core exposes a to_xarray() bridge to the xarray ecosystem, but these notebooks deliberately stay within pyramids-core's own GDAL-based UGRID I/O and do not use xarray.

    Takeaway¶

    • The geos driver reconstructs a GEOS cubed-sphere grid from its (6, C+1, C+1) corner arrays into a pyramids MeshDataset.
    • C12 cells are quadrilaterals (k = 4, 864 = 6×12×12) with coordinates in degrees — so circumcenters is skipped (triangles only).
    • connected_components recovers the six cube panels (144 cells each) — a direct readout of the cubed-sphere topology.
    • The rest of the pyramids GIS layer applies — to_geodataframe, bounding_polygon, adjacency, crop, PLY round-trip — while to_crs is skipped (no CRS recorded).
